analysis.one_liner: Strips the labor board of its power to order employers to bring back jobs moved or outsourced in retaliation.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 238-186, with 230 of 241 Republicans in favor, but the Senate never voted and it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes the National Labor Relations Act so that the National Labor Relations Board — the federal agency that enforces workers' rights to organize — could no longer order an employer to restore work it moved or outsourced, or to undo a relocation, even when that move was found to be retaliation against workers for union activity. It would have applied to complaints still pending when it passed. The bill came days after the labor board filed a high-profile complaint against Boeing over moving 787 production from Washington state to South Carolina, which is why it was often called the Boeing bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing labor-board cases over relocating or outsourcing work — the bill would wipe out the board's ability to make them restore the jobs, and it would apply to complaints already in progress.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the labor board's power to order an employer to restore work, reopen a production line, or rescind a relocation, transfer, subcontracting, or outsourcing decision.
Applies the change to any complaint for which the board had not yet made a final decision, wiping out remedies in cases already underway.
Also bars the board from requiring any employer to make an investment at a particular plant or facility.

analysis.who_pays: Workers whose jobs were moved or outsourced in retaliation for union activity would lose the board's remedy, retroactively.

drawbacks.text: The bill would apply retroactively to pending complaints, taking away remedies from workers whose cases were already before the board.

Supporters' strongest objection to keeping the existing rule: an order to restore work or keep a production line in a particular state, they argued, would make companies afraid to build new plants anywhere, chilling job creation — a concern an honest supporter of the bill's defeat acknowledges is a fair question about how far the board should go.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost of this bill falling on workers is real and retroactive: a company that moved work as retaliation would face no order to bring it back. Against that, the board's remedies in relocation cases are rare and legally contested, which is the strongest point for the bill. Weighed together, the bill tilts decisively toward employers facing enforcement, not workers.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a 238-186 party-line vote on September 15, 2011, but it was never brought to a vote in the Senate — it simply sat on the Senate calendar until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 19, 2011, and referred to the Education and Workforce Committee, which held a markup two days later and reported it amended on a 23-16 vote by July 25.
The Rules Committee set up floor consideration under a rule that closed the bill to amendments, with the committee substitute considered as adopted.

A Democratic motion to recommit with instructions — to add language preserving the board's authority to order employers to maintain or restore jobs being outsourced in violation of the act — failed 189-235, with 187 of 192 voting Democrats in favor and only 2 Republicans.
The bill passed the House 238-186: 230 of 241 voting Republicans in favor, only 8 of 192 voting Democrats.
The Senate received the bill and placed it on its calendar, but it never came to a vote, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions who rely on the labor board's remedies came out ahead, because the bill died in the Senate and the board kept its existing authority. Employers who would have benefited from the restriction gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers; the bill died in the Senate

for.name: Tim Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the labor board of its relocation remedies.

for.name: John Kline
for.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Moved the bill through committee within days of introduction — markup two days after referral, reported amended on a 23-16 vote.

for.name: John Boehner
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a rule that closed it to amendments.

against.name: 179 of 192 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, and 187 of them voted for the motion to preserve the board's authority over outsourced jobs.

against.name: Tim Bishop
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to protect the board's authority to order jobs restored in the United States; the motion failed 189-235.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the calendar.

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed the bill and threatened a veto as it moved through the House.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 230 of 241 voting Republicans yes versus 8 of 192 voting Democrats yes, and the failed motion to recommit was 187 Democratic yeas to 2 Republican yeas.

industries.industry: Manufacturers with unionized workforces (including aerospace employers like Boeing)
industries.note: The bill would remove the labor board's remedy when an employer moves, outsources, or closes work found to be retaliation against union activity, applying even to pending cases. It was widely understood as a response to the board's 2011 complaint against Boeing over shifting 787 production from Washington state to South Carolina, so employers facing similar complaints stood to benefit directly at the expense of the affected workers.

industries.industry: Labor unions and workers relying on board remedies
industries.note: Stripping the board's power to order reinstatement of relocated work would have taken away the main remedy available when job moves are used to punish organizing, including in cases already pending.
